describes: pistol, reads, runs. In the fourth, they are in the shotgun with four and five receivers, a team built
around the run trying to throw its way back from three scores. Tennessee's plan, as analysts described it at the
time, also included more defenders at the second level who could flow to the ball, a version of answer 1, but
the scoreboard did the most damage.[^balanswer]
:::

### Answer 3: pressure and zero

The third answer attacked the passing half of the bargain. If the box can't be made heavy enough to stop the run,
and the offense has fewer receivers than usual, send everyone. In a
[Cover 0](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-cover-0) pressure there is no deep safety; every defender either
rushes or covers a man, and the quarterback has to beat the blitz with a quick throw before it reaches him. Miami
did this to Jackson on a Thursday night in November 2021, blitzing on most of his dropbacks and
playing zero coverage behind it, and won easily against a team that had been 6–2.
[10-02](../10-situational-football/10-02-third-down.qmd) has the numbers and the film.

Why does it fit this offense? Zero coverage gives up the deep middle, and the quarterback is the man best
equipped to punish it by running, so it is a real gamble. But it also takes away the *time* a play-action pass
needs: a heavy formation's fake pulls linebackers up, but a blitzing linebacker was coming up anyway. The
Ravens' longer-term answer was the one the next sections describe: a passing game with more receivers who could
win quickly, built under a new coordinator.

### Answer 4: spy him and disguise it

The fourth answer is the most direct: assign one defender to Jackson, a
[**spy**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-spy), and hide which one. The Chiefs did it with linebacker Leo Chenal
in 2024; the Lions did it in 2025 with a plan their coordinator credited not to the spy but to making every
defender look the same before the snap. [10-02](../10-situational-football/10-02-third-down.qmd#the-spy)
tells both games. The cost of a spy is the cost of every answer in this list: a defender assigned to the quarterback
is not in coverage and not filling a gap, and against a running quarterback that is simply the price of admission.

### What the answers have in common

Look at the four together and a pattern appears. None of them *stopped* the run game for a season; the chart in
@fig-rush-epa says so. What they did was **make the Ravens play from behind, or make them throw against a
defense built to stop the throw**, in single games. That is the honest summary of the era's defensive history,
and it leads straight to the question every Ravens fan has argued about.

## The playoffs, honestly

From the 2018 season through 2024, the Ravens with Jackson at quarterback went `{python} str(LJ_PO_W)`–`{python} str(LJ_PO_L)`
in the playoffs and never reached a Super Bowl. "Can't win in January" became the era's caption. What does the data say?

```{python}
#| label: fig-playoffs
#| fig-cap: "Baltimore's nine playoff games, 2018–2024 seasons, against the regular season. Left: EPA per play in each game (filled dots are wins, open dots losses; the gray line is the Ravens' average across the Jackson-era regular seasons, from week 11 of 2018). The January 2023 game in Cincinnati was started by Tyler Huntley. Right: three things that separate the playoff games from the regular season: the share of snaps played while trailing by more than a touchdown, the share of plays that were designed runs, and turnovers per game. Data: nflverse play-by-play and schedules via nflreadpy."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(6.7, 3.4), gridspec_kw={"width_ratios": [1.45, 1]})
ax = axes[0]
ax.axhline(REG_LINE["epa"], color=style.MUTED, lw=1.4)
ax.text(8.45, REG_LINE["epa"] + 0.025, "regular season", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2, ha="right")
ax.axhline(0, color=style.BASELINE, lw=0.8)
for i, (gid, r) in enumerate(PO_LINES.iterrows()):
    won = r["bal"] > r["opp_pts"]
    ax.scatter(i, r["epa"], s=34, color=style.SERIES[0], facecolor=style.SERIES[0] if won else "white", lw=1.5,
               zorder=3)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(PO_LINES)),
              [f"{int(r.season)}\n{r.opp}" + ("*" if gid == "2022_19_BAL_CIN" else "") for gid, r in PO_LINES.iterrows()],
              fontsize=6.6)
ax.set_ylabel("EPA per play", fontsize=8)
ax.set_title("Each playoff game", fontsize=9)
ax.tick_params(axis="y", labelsize=7.5)
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
ax.set_ylim(-0.36, 0.36)
ax = axes[1]
labels = ["trailing by 8+", "designed runs", "turnovers / game"]
regv = [REG_LINE["trail8"], REG_LINE["run_rate"], REG_LINE["to"] / REG_GAMES]
pov = [POST_LINE["trail8"], POST_LINE["run_rate"], POST_LINE["to"] / len(PO_LINES)]
y = np.arange(3)[::-1]
ax.barh(y + 0.18, regv, height=0.34, color=style.MUTED, label="regular season")
ax.barh(y - 0.18, pov, height=0.34, color=style.SERIES[1], label="playoffs")
for yy, a, b, k in zip(y, regv, pov, range(3)):
    fa = (lambda v: f"{v:.1f}") if k == 2 else pct
    ax.text(a + 0.03, yy + 0.18, fa(a), va="center", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2)
    ax.text(b + 0.03, yy - 0.18, fa(b), va="center", fontsize=7, color=style.INK_2)
ax.set_yticks(y, labels, fontsize=7.5)
ax.set_xlim(0, 2.3)
ax.set_xticks([])
ax.grid(False)
ax.spines["bottom"].set_visible(False)
ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc="upper right")
ax.set_title("What changed", fontsize=9)
fig.tight_layout(w_pad=1.0)
plt.show()
```

Three readings, from least to most important.

**The offense was worse in the playoffs, a lot worse.** Across the Jackson-era regular seasons the Ravens averaged
`{python} sg(REG_LINE["epa"], 3)` EPA per play, an elite offense. In their nine playoff games they averaged
`{python} sg(POST_LINE["epa"], 3)`, roughly an average one, and their designed runs went from
`{python} sg(REG_LINE["run_epa"])` per play to `{python} sg(POST_LINE["run_epa"])`. That part of the
narrative is true. Playoff opponents are better than regular-season ones, and the Ravens' playoff opponents had
time to prepare for an offense unlike anyone else's, but the drop is bigger than either explains on its own.

**The losses came from falling behind and giving the ball away.** The right panel is the mechanism. In the regular
season the Ravens trailed by more than a touchdown on only `{python} pct(REG_LINE["trail8"])` of their snaps; in the
playoffs, on `{python} pct(POST_LINE["trail8"])`. They turned the ball over
`{python} f"{REG_LINE['to'] / REG_GAMES:.1f}"` times a game in the regular season and
`{python} f"{POST_LINE['to'] / len(PO_LINES):.1f}"` in the playoffs, three in four of the six losses. And
trailing changes the offense: the share of designed runs fell from `{python} pct(REG_LINE["run_rate"])` to
`{python} pct(POST_LINE["run_rate"])`. This is answer 2 from the last section, playing out across a decade: a run
game built to win close games was asked, again and again, to win from behind.

**The run game was rarely the reason.** Look at the losses one at a time. Against the Chargers in 2019 and the
Titans in 2020 the run game was stuffed, but both games were decided by early deficits and turnovers. In the
January 2024 AFC Championship against Kansas City, the Ravens trailed 17–7 at halftime and ran only 16 times all
game, with their running backs carrying six of them; their designed runs averaged
`{python} sg(PO_LINES.loc["2023_21_KC_BAL", "run_epa"])` EPA, better than their regular-season average, and they
lost 17–10 after three turnovers.[^afcg] In January 2025 at Buffalo they ran for 176 yards and still lost 27–25,
after an interception, a fumble on a sack and a Mark Andrews fumble, then a failed two-point conversion that
would have tied the game.[^buf25] The playoff losses look less like a scheme being solved and more like an
offense built on the run being taken out of it by the scoreboard.

How much of that is bad luck? Some, certainly: nine games, about `{python} f"{int(POST_LINE['plays']):,}"` plays,
is a small sample, and turnovers in particular are noisy from game to game. But a pattern repeated across six
seasons, four lead running backs and three coordinators deserves an explanation, and the most honest one is this: the
pistol option offense was at its best protecting a lead or playing even, and the games it lost were the games where
it had to do the thing it was built to do least. The 2023 change of coordinator was, in part, an attempt to fix
exactly that.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game, a great offense is great in every situation, because you can call any play from any score. Real
offenses are built for a *range* of situations: personnel, practice time and a quarterback's skills all get spent
on the situations the staff expects most. An offense built to run is spending its practice week on runs, and when
it falls behind by fourteen, it is asking players to win with the part of the playbook they practised least. That
is a trade-off, not a flaw, and every offense makes one.
:::

## The Monken changes (2023)

After the 2022 season Greg Roman left. The Ravens' offense under him had ranked first, seventh, 17th and 19th in
points in his four years as coordinator, and the passing game had never quite caught up to the run.[^romanexit]
In February 2023 Baltimore hired **Todd Monken**, who had just won two straight national championships as
Georgia's offensive coordinator and had run NFL offenses in Tampa Bay and Cleveland.[^monken]

Monken's mandate was to make Jackson a quarterback who could win from the pocket, without throwing away what made
him dangerous. @fig-fingerprint shows what he did:

- **From the pistol to the shotgun.** Pistol snaps fell from `{python} pct(QBLOC.loc[(2022, True), "P"])` of plays
  in 2022 to `{python} pct(QBLOC.loc[(2023, True), "P"])` in 2023, and the shotgun rose to
  `{python} pct(QBLOC.loc[(2023, True), "S"])`.[^loc] The shotgun gives the quarterback a better view of the
  coverage and a faster launch, at the cost of the pistol's downhill back and its lack of a tell.
- **Fewer designed quarterback runs.** Jackson's designed runs fell from `{python} f"{LJ_PG.loc[2022]:.1f}"` a game to
  `{python} f"{LJ_PG.loc[2023]:.1f}"`. He still ran, but more of it was scrambling, improvising when a pass play broke
  down, rather than running on purpose.
- **More receivers, and more passing on early downs.** The Ravens drafted receiver Zay Flowers in the first round,
  used three-receiver sets more, and on neutral early downs ran the ball on `{python} pct(NEU_BAL.loc[2023])` of
  plays, `{python} ordinal(NEU_RANK.loc[2023])` in the league, after ranking first in that category in 2019.

The result was a career-high 3,678 passing yards for Jackson and his second MVP award, won with 49 of 50 first-place
votes, and a `{python} rec(2023)` record and the AFC's top seed.[^mvp23] The run game didn't collapse without the
volume of quarterback runs. It ranked `{python} ordinal(BAL_RUN.loc[2023, "rank"])` in EPA per designed run, and the
Ravens still led the league in rushing yards. The threat was doing the work the carries used to do: a backside end
who had to respect Jackson every snap was still frozen, whether Jackson ran six times or four.

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: AFC Championship, Kansas City at Baltimore, January 28, 2024"}
The Ravens beat Houston 34–10 in the divisional round, then hosted the Chiefs for a trip to the Super Bowl. They lost
17–10, and the game became the sharpest criticism of the Monken offense: Baltimore ran only 16 times, and its
running backs carried just six of those.[^afcg2]

**What to notice:** the first half and the turnovers, not the play-calling alone. Kansas City led 17–7 at halftime,
and the Ravens turned the ball over three times: a fumble on a sack in the second quarter, then, in the fourth, Zay
Flowers's fumble at the Kansas City 1-yard line and an interception in the end zone. Watch Steve Spagnuolo's defense on Jackson's dropbacks: four-man rushes,
disguised coverages, and rushers who kept their lanes so that Jackson's scrambles went nowhere. Then ask the question
the chapter keeps asking: was the run abandoned, or was it taken away by the scoreboard? The answer is some of both,
and it was the last time the Ravens' run game rested mainly on Jackson.
:::

## The Derrick Henry seasons (2024–2025)

In March 2024 the Ravens signed **Derrick Henry**, the 30-year-old former Titans back who had run for 2,027 yards
in 2020 and had beaten them almost single-handedly in that January 2020 playoff game, on a two-year
contract.[^henry] It was a signing that made the threat run both ways. For five years, defenses had to decide whom to
fear on a read: the quarterback or a good running back. Now the back was one of the most punishing runners of his
generation, a 247-pound back who had led the league in rushing twice.

**2024 was the best offense of the era.** Henry ran for 1,921 yards and 16 touchdowns, second in the league in
yards behind Saquon Barkley's 2,005; Jackson threw for 4,172 yards, 41 touchdowns and only four interceptions; and
Baltimore led the NFL in EPA per play, in rushing yards, and, again, in EPA per designed run.[^h24] The team went
`{python} rec(2024)`, beat Pittsburgh in the wild-card round as Henry ran for 186 yards, and lost at Buffalo,
the game described above.

**The run game moved under center.** The data shows how differently the Henry offense was built. The Ravens took
`{python} pct(QBLOC.loc[(2024, True), "U"])` of their 2024 snaps with Jackson under center, nearly three times their
2022 rate, and `{python} pct(BAL_RUN_UC.loc[2024])` of their designed runs started there. Henry is a downhill back who
wants to hit the line with speed, and taking the snap under center lets him get the ball deep in the backfield,
running forward, on zone, duo and gap runs, with play-action passes built off the same look. The read game didn't
vanish; it got rarer, and it kept its best form. Henry's carries from the pistol, `{python} str(int(HENRY_LOC.loc["P", "n"]))`
of them across the two seasons, averaged `{python} f"{HENRY_LOC.loc['P', 'ypc']:.1f}"` yards and
`{python} sg(HENRY_LOC.loc["P", "epa"])` EPA, against `{python} f"{HENRY_LOC.loc['U', 'ypc']:.1f}"` yards and
`{python} sg(HENRY_LOC.loc["U", "epa"])` EPA from under center.[^henryloc] The small pistol sample is the read
offense in miniature: an end who has to stay home for Jackson is an end who isn't chasing Henry.

**2025 was the end.** Jackson missed four games, three with a hamstring injury in October and one with a back
injury in December, and was less of a runner when he played, saying afterwards that his health had limited his
mobility:[^lj25] by this chapter's count `{python} str(LJ_N.loc[2025])` designed runs in
`{python} str(LJ_GAMES.loc[2025])` games, about two a game.
Henry still ran for more than 1,500 yards, the run game still ranked `{python} ordinal(BAL_RUN.loc[2025, "rank"])` in
EPA per designed run, and the Ravens ran on early downs more than all but one team. But a 1–5 start, a defense that
gave up 398 points, and a 26–24 loss at Pittsburgh in Week 18 with the division on the line left them
`{python} rec(2025)` and out of the playoffs.[^s25] On January 6, 2026, the Ravens fired John Harbaugh after 18
seasons.

## What survives: the era closed, and the 2026 epilogue

The coaches have scattered. Harbaugh is the Giants' head coach in 2026, Monken is the Browns' head coach, and Roman
spent 2024 and 2025 as Jim Harbaugh's offensive coordinator with the Chargers, who fired him in
January 2026.[^roman26] The 2026 Ravens belong to **Jesse Minter**, a Ravens assistant from 2017 to 2020 and the Chargers'
defensive coordinator in 2024 and 2025, as head
coach, with **Declan Doyle**, who came from Ben Johnson's Chicago staff, as offensive coordinator and **Anthony
Weaver** as defensive coordinator.[^staff2026] Jackson is still the quarterback. What Doyle builds around him is a
2026 story, and this chapter stops at the end of 2025.

What survives the era is bigger than one team.

- **The arithmetic is now conventional wisdom.** "Count the quarterback as a blocker" was an option coach's slogan
  in 2018. By 2025 it was how every NFL defense planned for Jalen Hurts, Josh Allen and Jayden Daniels, and how every
  analyst explained why those offenses ran well against light boxes.
- **Heavy personnel came back.** In 2025 NFL offenses used fewer than three receivers on 41.7% of plays, the most
  since Next Gen Stats began tracking.[^heavy25] The Ravens weren't the only cause (the 49ers, Rams and Eagles all
  pushed the same way), but they showed that a modern offense could live in 12, 21 and 22 personnel and still throw.
- **The quarterback run became a managed resource.** The Ravens' own data tells the story of the last seven years in
  miniature: from seven or eight designed runs a game in 2019 to about two in 2025, with the efficiency of the run
  game barely moving. The lesson the league took is that a running quarterback's value is mostly in the *threat*,
  which can be spent a few carries at a time, on the downs and in the games where it matters, and saved the rest of
  the time.
- **The pistol didn't.** The pistol as a *base* alignment was a Ravens thing, and it left with Roman. It survives as a
  run-heavy niche look (02-02's data has a few teams living in it), and as the backfield of choice for read plays
  from under-center teams. That is a good example of the course's larger point: the principle (an extra blocker,
  either side, no tell) outlived its favourite formation.

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it"}
**On Sunday: count the defenders against a running quarterback.** Any team with a quarterback who runs, Baltimore
or not, will do.

*Before the snap*

- **Count the blockers:** five linemen, plus every tight end and fullback near the line.
- **Count the box:** the [box count](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-box-count) is every defender within about five yards of the ball and inside the tight ends.
- **Add the quarterback.** If he's in the pistol or shotgun with a back beside or behind him and is a real runner,
  add one to the offense's side. Now compare: more defenders than blockers-plus-one, and the defense has its
  plus-one; even, and the defense's extra man has to come from a safety.
- **Find where the extra man is.** A safety walked down at eight yards, or a single deep safety in the middle? Then
  the play-action pass is aimed at him.
- **Where is the back?** Directly behind the quarterback (pistol): no directional tell. Beside him: note the side,
  and expect the run (or the read) to go the other way.

*At the snap*

- **Watch the two ends.** The one nobody touches is being read. Does he stay home (give coming) or chase (keep
  coming)?
- **Look for a puller.** A guard pulling toward the unblocked end: power read. A guard and a tight end pulling the
  same way while the quarterback steps the other way: QB counter.

*After the play*

- On the replay, check the backside end on a plain handoff. Did he chase the cutback, or stay home for a quarterback
  who didn't have the ball? Count how often he stays, over a quarter. That is the hidden yardage.
- Note the score. Is the offense still running when it's behind by two scores? That's the question that decided the
  Ravens' playoff games.
:::

## Predict the play

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 1: eight in the box.** First-and-10 at midfield, first quarter, tied. Baltimore is in the pistol with two
tight ends; the defense walks a safety down and shows eight in the box with one deep safety. Count the blockers
and the box with Jackson as a runner. Who is the defense's extra man, and which Ravens play does this picture
invite?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-1
#| fig-cap: "Drill 1: pistol 12 personnel against an eight-man box and a single deep safety (the wide receivers and cornerbacks are out of the picture)."
p = Play(pistol(), front62(fs=True), los=60, to_go=10, title="Drill 1: 1st and 10, midfield")
f = draw(p, lateral=(-10.0, 10.0), window=(-8.6, 14.6), width_in=4.8)
box_shade(f, p, 0.2, 5.6, -7.6, 7.6)
plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Seven blockers plus Jackson's read against eight: a hat on every hat.** Five linemen and two tight ends make seven
blockers. The box has eight: six on the line and two linebackers. On a handoff with a pocket quarterback the defense
would be plus-one. With Jackson reading one end, it is even (@fig-fit-two-qbs, @fig-pistol-iv).

**The defense's extra man is the free safety**, the only defender not in the box and the only one deep. If he comes
down to stop the run, there is nobody behind the linebackers.

**What it invites:** any of the reads, which is the point of the arithmetic, but most of all a **play-action pass at
the deep middle**. Eight in the box against the Ravens meant the defense had spent its last spare man; a fake to the
back that holds the linebackers and the safety for a beat, with a tight end up the seam behind them, is the play this
picture is begging for (@fig-13-plate, left).
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 2: read the 9.** Same look, a moment after the snap. The line is blocking power to the right: the tight end
and tackle have blocked down, the left guard is pulling. The play-side 9 has not been touched. He has stepped
hard *inside*, toward the hole. The back is sweeping right across Jackson's face. Give or keep? And if the read is
right, who has to make the tackle?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-2
#| fig-cap: "Drill 2: the pistol power read a moment after the snap. The play-side 9 (ringed) has squeezed inside (his short arrow); the line's blocks are drawn, and the back (thin arrow) is sweeping right."
dfn = [q.moved(d=0.9, w=5.4) if q.key == "PE" else q for q in front62(fs=True)]
p = Play(pistol(), dfn, los=60, to_go=10, title="Drill 2: the 9 squeezes")
go_to(p, "Y", (0.4, 4.1), via=[(-0.3, 4.5)])
go_to(p, "RT", (0.5, 2.7), via=[(-0.4, 3.0)])
go_to(p, "RG", (1.6, 1.0), via=[(-0.2, 1.9), (0.4, 2.0)])
go_to(p, "C", (0.4, -0.5))
go_to(p, "LT", (0.3, -3.8), via=[(-0.6, -3.5)])
go_to(p, "U", (0.4, -6.0), via=[(-0.4, -5.3)])
go_to(p, "LG", (-1.9, 2.2), "pull", via=[(-1.7, -1.2)])
go_to(p, "RB", (-4.8, 3.6), "path", via=[(-5.6, 1.2)])
p.highlight("PE", color=style.DEFENSE)
f = draw(p, lateral=(-10.0, 13.0), window=(-8.6, 14.2), width_in=5.0)
x0, y0 = _P(f, p, 1.6, 7.6)
x1, y1 = _P(f, p, 1.2, 6.3)
f.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch((float(x0), float(y0)), (float(x1), float(y1)), arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10,
                               color=style.DEFENSE, lw=1.6, zorder=6))
point_to(f, p, (4.2, 9.6), (1.5, 7.2), "the 9 squeezes\ninside", color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, fontsize=6.8)
read_line(f, p, (-4.0, 0.3), (0.6, 5.0))
plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**Give.** The 9 has squeezed inside, toward the hole the quarterback would run through: he has taken the keep away
himself. So Jackson hands the ball to the back, who is already running outside the 9 at full speed (@fig-pistol-iv).

**Who has to tackle him?** Nobody in the box: every other box defender is blocked, and the 9 is inside the runner.
The tackle has to come from **outside or behind**: the cornerback on that side (if the wide receiver hasn't blocked
him) or the free safety, coming from 12 yards deep across the field. That is the power read's promise, a running
back in space against a defensive back, and its risk: if the corner or safety arrives in time and the back was
running sideways, the gain is small.

If the 9 had **widened** with the back instead, the answer flips: keep, and Jackson runs inside him behind the
pulling guard.
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Predict the play"}
**Drill 3: down fourteen.** Second-and-8 at your own 30, early in the third quarter of a playoff game. You're down 14.
The defense shows two deep safeties and only six in the box. Your quarterback is a great runner; your offense has
the league's best run game. Does the box say run? Does the scoreboard? What would you call, and what does the
Ravens' history say about the trap in this picture?

```{python}
#| label: fig-drill-3
#| fig-cap: "Drill 3: shotgun 11 personnel (one tight end, three receivers) against a two-high shell with six in the box; the offense is down 14 early in the third quarter."
off = line5() + [O("QB", "QB", -5.0, 0.0, "Q"), O("RB", "RB", -5.0, 2.1, "R"), O("Y", "TE", -0.7, 4.8, "Y"),
                 O("X", "WR", -0.7, -15.0, "X"), O("H", "WR", -1.5, -9.0, "H"), O("Z", "WR", -1.5, 14.5, "Z")]
check_legal(off)
dfn = [D("LE", "DE", 1.0, -4.1, "5"), D("DT1", "DT", 1.0, -0.7, "1"), D("DT3", "DT", 1.0, 2.4, "3"),
       D("RE", "DE", 1.0, 5.6, "9"), D("MIKE", "MIKE", 5.0, 1.6, "M"), D("WILL", "WILL", 5.0, -2.4, "W"),
       D("NB", "NB", 5.0, -8.6, "NB"), D("LCB", "CB", 7.0, -15.0, "CB"), D("RCB", "CB", 7.0, 14.5, "CB"),
       D("FS", "FS", 13.0, -7.0, "FS"), D("SS", "SS", 13.0, 7.0, "SS")]
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=8, title="Drill 3: 2nd and 8, down 14, third quarter")
f = draw(p, lateral=(-18.0, 17.5), window=(-8.0, 15.6), width_in=5.6)
box_shade(f, p, 0.2, 6.0, -6.4, 7.0)
plt.show()
```
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The box says run.** It is a [light box](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-light-box): six defenders against six blockers (five linemen and the tight end) and a quarterback who reads:
the offense is effectively plus-one. Against light boxes, efficient running teams do well, and the Ravens were the most
efficient running team of their era (@fig-rush-epa).

**The scoreboard says "don't panic."** Down 14 with more than a quarter and a half to play is two possessions, not a
two-minute drill. A good run on second-and-8 is a good play in any quarter, and an offense built on the run that
abandons it at the first deficit plays into the defense's hands, which is exactly what this two-high shell is
inviting: if you throw against two deep safeties and six underneath, you are throwing into the coverage the defense
chose. (The win-probability tools of [13-03](../13-analytics-and-data/13-03-win-probability-and-fourth-down.qmd) make
this precise.)

**The trap** is the one in @fig-playoffs. Deficits pushed the Ravens out of their offense in the playoffs (their
designed-run share fell from about `{python} pct(REG_LINE["run_rate"])` to `{python} pct(POST_LINE["run_rate"])`),
and turnovers, more common when a run team throws from behind, made the deficits bigger. The right call here is
probably the run the defense is conceding (a read, or a designed run with the back blocking), and the right *plan*
is to stay patient for another series. The two-score deficit becomes a three-score deficit far more often from an
interception than from a three-yard run.
:::

## Takeaways

- The 2019–2022 Ravens built a **pistol option offense**: the pistol as the base alignment, heavy personnel, a menu of
  option reads and designed quarterback runs, so that the defense had to account for one more ball carrier on every
  snap.
- A running quarterback changes **every** run fit, not just the reads: the end he might read has to stay home on plain
  handoffs too, every defender's fit gets a "quarterback" line, and backside pursuit stops being free. An eight-man
  box against him is a seven-man box.
- The signature plays each make a defender's textbook reaction wrong: the **pistol inverted veer** (squeeze the hole
  and the back runs outside you), **13 personnel** (play it as a run formation and the seam opens; Baltimore threw
  from it two times in three), and the **QB counter** (follow the first flow and the play goes back the other way).
- The data fingerprint: Baltimore's designed runs were above the league average **every season** from 2018 to 2025,
  top three in six of them, under two coordinators and five lead backs. What changed was the recipe: pistol and
  quarterback runs under Roman, the shotgun and fewer designed runs under **Monken (2023)**, under-center runs with
  **Derrick Henry (2024–2025)**.
- Defenses answered with speed, pressure, spies and, most effectively, **the scoreboard**. The playoff record (3–5 with
  Jackson) came mostly from early deficits and turnovers that pulled a run-first offense away from the run, not from
  the run game being solved.
- The era closed in January 2026 with Harbaugh's firing. What survives is the arithmetic (count the quarterback as a
  blocker), heavy personnel, and the idea that a running quarterback's value is mostly the threat, spent a few carries
  at a time.

::: {.callout-note title="Go deeper"}
**From the simulation to real tracking data.** The QB counter animation in this chapter is a gridiron simulation
written in NFL Big Data Bowl coordinates (simulated, BDB-format), so real tracking frames drop into the same drawing
code. The Big Data Bowl releases carry the play-by-play description of each play, so finding a Jackson designed run
is a text search (`"L.Jackson"` as the rusher, no "scramble"), and the pre-snap frames of the 2025 edition show
whether he was in the pistol. The cell below, folded on the website and not run (the course does not download the
Big Data Bowl files), shows the shape of that code.

```{python}
#| eval: false
#| code-summary: "Show the Python (real tracking data; not run)"
import pandas as pd
from gridiron import bdb, show_animation

trk = bdb.load_tracking("data/bdb/tracking_week_*.csv")       # BDB 2025: 2022 season, weeks 1-9
plays = pd.read_csv("data/bdb/plays.csv")
runs = plays[(plays["possessionTeam"] == "BAL") & plays["playDescription"].str.contains("L.Jackson")
             & ~plays["playDescription"].str.contains("scramble|pass", case=False)]
one = bdb.prepare(trk, plays, game_id=runs["gameId"].iloc[0], play_id=runs["playId"].iloc[0])
show_animation(one, times=[0.0, 0.6, 1.3, 2.1])                 # the same four moments as the simulation
```
:::
